statement:
Let $n$ be a positive integer.

(i) Factorise $n^5-n^3$, and show that it is divisible by $24$.

(ii) Prove that $2^{2n}-1$ is divisible by $3$.

(iii) If $n-1$ is divisible by $3$, show that $n^3-1$ is divisible by $9$.
solution:
(i) Factorise:
$$n^5-n^3=n^3(n^2-1)=n^3(n-1)(n+1).$$

Since $(n-1)n(n+1)$ is the product of three consecutive integers, it is divisible by $3$ (one of the three is a multiple of $3$) and by $2$ (at least one is even). In fact $n^3(n-1)(n+1)=n^2\cdot n(n-1)(n+1)$ is divisible by $8$: if $n$ is even then $n^3$ contains $2^3$; if $n$ is odd then $(n-1)(n+1)$ is the product of two consecutive even numbers, which is divisible by $8$. Together with the factor $3$, the product is divisible by $8\times3=24$.

(ii) Write $2^{2n}-1=4^n-1$. Since $4\equiv1\pmod3$, we have $4^n\equiv1^n=1\pmod3$, so $4^n-1\equiv0\pmod3$. Hence $2^{2n}-1$ is divisible by $3$.

(iii) Since $n-1$ is divisible by $3$, write $n=3k+1$. Then
$$n^3-1=(n-1)(n^2+n+1).$$
Now $n-1=3k$ is divisible by $3$. Also $n^2+n+1=(3k+1)^2+(3k+1)+1=9k^2+9k+3=3(3k^2+3k+1)$, which is divisible by $3$. Since both factors are divisible by $3$, their product $n^3-1$ is divisible by $9$.
hints: Factorise n^5-n^3 as n^3(n-1)(n+1) and use divisibility of consecutive integers.
For (iii), write n=3k+1 and factor n^3-1.
